html:
What this is

The Symbolic World is a map of C. G. Jung's symbolic thought: 1156 symbols, figures and concepts, joined by 4829 relations, resting on 6480 citations to his Collected Works (CW). One AI model (Opus family) proposed each claim from a window of paragraphs, and a model of a different family (Fable) judged it against its source paragraph. An auditor from another vendor (Google's Gemini) then re-read the result: 98% of the 6480 citations carry an audit stamp, and all but 14 of the stamps name the audit and its date. Each claim is a ledger entry: the exact paragraph, a verbatim quote, and a record of which model, or which person, checked what. This is a map of assertions, not a Jungian reading.

A relation joins two nodes. Each citation that supports it, a paragraph with its quote, is one claim, so a relation can rest on several.

Read it as: Jung says, at paragraph 264 of Aion, that the stone (lapis) is a projection of the self. Clicking the claim in the atlas shows the quote.

One corpus

Everything comes from a single source: the Bollingen edition of the Collected Works, in English. No secondary literature, no commentary, no symbol dictionaries. That keeps the map close to Jung's own text, at the cost of breadth.

Click a segment and the atlas shows only that volume's claims.

Reading the atlas

Node colour shows the kind of node. The palette borrows alchemy's metals: gold for concepts, silver for symbols, copper for figures, iron for operations, verdigris for substances, lead for motifs. Alchemy assigned its metals to the planets. Assigning them to node kinds is our design choice and carries no alchemical meaning.

  • Search finds a symbol, a relation, a family, quote text, or a citation such as CW 14 §1. Typing offers completions, and choosing a symbol or a family opens it.
  • Click a node to read its connections; click a connection to open the citation itself: relation, quote, paragraph, verdicts. Copy link on any selection gives a URL that reopens it.
  • The chips beside the search box are the active filters: volume, family, voice, layer. Remove one with its ×.
  • Every citation shows a status dot: green, human-validated; amber, machine-verified default without human validation; red, disputed, on the record. The ledger lists all three.

How a claim gets in

  1. Propose. An Opus-family model reads a window of consecutive paragraphs and proposes claims, each with a verbatim citation.
  2. Check. A machine confirms the quote is letter-exact in its paragraph and at most 25 words, and that the claim has the form of one relation between two nodes. The pipeline drops claims that fail.
  3. Gate. A Fable-family model judges every claim against its full source paragraph. Its instructions make rejection the default: a claim survives only if the model finds that the paragraph supports it.
  4. Audit. A Gemini model re-reads every claim that survived the gate, before it enters the graph. The step became the rule in mid-2026, when work on Aion began. Later passes audited the older material, by whole volumes and by samples, and each citation's stamp says which. 6377 of 6480 citations carry a stamp. The other 103, in Aion and the volumes mined after it, have none yet, and the record does not say why. Where gate and auditor disagree on whether the paragraph supports the claim, the auditor's verdict stands. Findings about claim type or confidence become corrections, and a recorded project convention can overrule the auditor; the claim's record then shows the override.
  5. Merge. The claim enters with its provenance stamped: dates, verdicts, corrections.

At every step, the model that proposes a claim never signs it off. Proposer and gate are different model families (Anthropic's Opus and Fable lines) and the auditor is a different vendor (Google's Gemini).

The checks remove real material: across the 86 windows whose records give both counts, 5557 proposed citations became 5175 merged ones.

Human oversight

One person, the author, rules on disagreements, decides releases and answers for everything the site publishes.

  • Validated by a person. 50 claims carry a human-validated mark in the ledger: a person read the cited paragraph. The rest carry the amber dot: machine-verified without human validation.
  • Adjudication. Two models sort each relation into one of 25 families, working blind: one Opus-family model and one Gemini, each given the definitions and the claim, neither able to see the other's answer. A Fable-family model drafted the definitions; neither classifying model comes from that family. 838 relations wait for a person's ruling, most because the two models disagreed, a few because a later check disputed their agreement. No model breaks a tie. A person rules on each one, and the ruling goes into the ledger. An assignment is recorded with the ruleset version it was agreed under, because a later version can retire the rule it rested on.
  • We count two kinds of unclassified relation separately. No family means none of our families fits. Text undecided means Jung's sentence supports two readings. Counting them together would hide gaps in our vocabulary among real ambiguities in the text.
  • Disputes. 18 challenges are on the record with their outcomes, in the dispute log.

How we test the checks

  • Every one of the 6480 quotes is mechanically verified against the corpus. The verification set seeds seven deliberately corrupted claims. So far, all seven have been caught on every run. Whether a paragraph supports its claim stays a model's judgment, which the gate and the auditor make independently.
  • The family gate faces the same kind of test: we plant corrupted assignments among real ones. At ruleset v0.7.2 it caught 19 of 19 planted errors and left 39 of 41 clean assignments alone. The gate is a Gemini model, as is one of the two classifying models. A family label means two models, judging independently, put the relation in that family, or a person ruled where they disagreed.
  • We checked the classification vocabulary against 8 published works of Jung scholarship. Where the literature discusses a relation at all (16 cases), scholars' readings matched our family in 8, differed in 6 and were split in 2. The design page lists the disagreements and the rule changes they produced. The check tests our sorting of relations into families. It says nothing about whether a claim is true.
  • The two classifying models agreed on 3953 of 4814 relations (82.1%): the relations whose record shows either their agreement or a disagreement for a person to settle. The other 15 rest on a precedent or on a later check. Agreement shows whether two readers apply the definitions the same way. It does not show that the definitions are right: neither model is authoritative.

What the instruments do not cover:

Known limitWhat would close it, or what offsets it
One human reviewer; no second annotator yetIndependent second annotation with agreement statistics
Nothing measures recall: every check tests what entered the map, and none estimates what Jung asserts that the map lacksA sampled audit of recall, paragraph by paragraph
A class of identity drift (two names for one thing entering as two things) is invisible to the current auditNo instrument yet
English translation only (Hull)German cross-check against the Gesammelte Werke
Claims are checked at paragraph granularity; fidelity to Jung's movement of thought across an essay or volume is not checkedPartly offset: where Jung qualifies a claim, the map records the qualifying claim too. A reading of the essay or volume is still needed

The paper

The method was published with release v1.3.0: 248 symbols, 669 relations, 699 citations. That exact snapshot, atlas and ledger included, is preserved unchanged at /v1.3/. The live counts at the top of every page show how far the atlas has grown since. The checks grew too: the relation families and the form rule for relations came after v1.3.0.

Trust, Layered: Warranted AI Knowledge Extraction for Interpretive Corpora, Demonstrated on Jung's Collected Works (dataset, pipeline, and paper)
